newsitem.title: USA: Groundhog fails to see shadow; spring 6 weeks away?.
newsitem.headline: Groundhog fails to see shadow; spring 6 weeks away?.

text.p: Spectators cheered and shed their coats and hats Sunday after Punxsutawney, Pa.'s most famous groundhog failed to see his shadow, a sign that spring is just around the corner.
Legend has it that if Punxsutawney Phil sees his shadow on Groundhog Day Feb. 2, winter will last six more weeks.
"This is only the 13th time in 110 years that Phil has not seen his shadow," said Nanci Puchy, executive director of the Punxsutawney Chamber of Commerce.
Puchy said Phil -- brown, furry and weighing in at 15 pounds -- has a 59 percent accuracy rate.

A record crowd of 35,000 spectators came to Punxsutawney Sunday to see the famous groundhog and join the media circus. The annual ceremony is held at Gobbler's Knob, which local residents refer to as Phil's "home."

The use of groundhogs as weather prophets can be traced to German and Scottish immigrants, Puchy said. According to Pennsylvania records, people began observing Groundhog Day in the early 1880s. A small group of residents would travel into the woods to spot the creatures.
The first trek to Gobbler's Knob to observe the tradition was Feb. 2, 1887.
Bill Deeley, Gobbler's Knob official "groundhog handler" who carries Phil to give spectators a close-up view, said Sunday's ceremony marked the largest turnout ever.
Groundhogs are bred in Punxsutawney to ensure every Groundhog Day has a groundhog.
